stem: The presentation of data means:
options: displaying the organised data in an attractive, understandable form — using text, tables, or diagrams/graphs
solution: The presentation of data means displaying/showing the organised (classified) data in an attractive, clear, and easily-understandable form — so that its meaning and patterns can be readily grasped. Data can be presented in three main ways: (1) textual/descriptive presentation (in the form of text/paragraphs); (2) tabular presentation (in tables — rows and columns); and (3) diagrammatic/graphical presentation (using diagrams and graphs — bar diagrams, pie charts, line graphs, histograms, etc.). Good presentation makes the data appealing and easy to understand, compare, and interpret. Presentation is the stage between the organisation and the analysis of data. Understanding what presentation of data means is a prelims-relevant point. Presentation of data is the displaying of organised data in an attractive, understandable form (text, tables, or diagrams/graphs).

stem: The three main forms/methods of presenting data are textual (descriptive), tabular, and:
solution: The three main forms/methods of presenting data are: (1) textual (descriptive) presentation — presenting the data as part of the text/in paragraphs (describing the figures in words); (2) tabular presentation — presenting the data in tables (arranged in rows and columns); and (3) diagrammatic/graphical presentation — presenting the data through diagrams and graphs (such as bar diagrams, pie charts, line graphs, and histograms). Each has its uses: textual for small amounts of data or emphasis, tabular for organised detail and comparison, and diagrammatic/graphical for visual appeal and quick understanding of patterns. Understanding the three forms of data presentation is a prelims-relevant point. The three main forms of presenting data are textual (descriptive), tabular, and diagrammatic/graphical.

stem: Presenting data in the form of a table (arranged systematically in rows and columns) is called __________ presentation.
solution: Tabular presentation is the presentation of data in the form of a table — arranging the data systematically in rows and columns (with headings/labels), according to some logical order and classification. A table condenses and organises the data compactly, making it easy to read, compare, and understand the figures (and to locate specific values). Tabulation is a very common and useful method of presenting statistical data, especially when there is a fair amount of data to be shown in an orderly, detailed way. Understanding tabular presentation is a prelims-relevant point. Tabular presentation is the presentation of data in a table, arranged in rows and columns.

stem: In a statistical table, the horizontal arrangements of data are called rows, and the vertical arrangements are called:
solution: In a statistical table, the data are arranged in two directions: the horizontal arrangements (going across) are called rows, and the vertical arrangements (going up and down) are called columns. The data are entered in the cells formed by the intersection of the rows and columns. (The headings of the rows are called 'stubs', and the headings of the columns are called 'captions' or 'column headings'.) So rows go across (horizontal) and columns go down (vertical). Understanding rows and columns in a table is a prelims-relevant point. In a table, the horizontal arrangements are rows and the vertical arrangements are columns.

stem: Every statistical table must have a __________ that clearly tells what the table is about.
solution: Every statistical table must have a title (heading) — a clear, brief, and self-explanatory heading (usually at the top of the table) that tells the reader exactly what the table is about (what data it contains, and often for what place and time period). A good title enables the reader to understand the contents of the table at a glance, without having to read all the details. (Along with the title, a table has other parts — the table number, the head-note, the column headings/captions, the row headings/stubs, the body/data, and, below, the footnotes and the source.) Understanding that a table must have a title is a prelims-relevant point. Every statistical table must have a title (heading) that clearly tells what the table is about.

stem: The __________ of a table (given at the bottom) tells the reader where the data in the table came from (the origin of the data).
solution: The source note (source) of a table — given at the bottom of the table (below the body and any footnotes) — tells the reader where the data presented in the table came from — i.e., the origin/source of the data (for example, the publication, agency, report, or survey from which the figures were taken). Stating the source is important because it lets the reader judge the reliability of the data, refer to the original for more detail, and know that the figures are authentic (not made up). So the source note credits and identifies the origin of the data. Understanding the source note of a table is a prelims-relevant point. The source note (at the bottom of a table) tells the reader where the data came from (the source/origin of the data).

stem: Explanatory notes at the bottom of a table that clarify some specific point or entry in the table are called:
solution: Footnotes are the explanatory notes given at the bottom of a table (below the body of the table, usually above the source note) that clarify or explain some specific point, entry, or feature of the table that is not clear from the table itself. For example, a footnote might explain the meaning of a symbol used, note that a particular figure is provisional/estimated, or explain a special case. Footnotes (often marked with symbols like *, †, or numbers) help the reader correctly understand and interpret specific items in the table. Understanding footnotes (clarifying notes in a table) is a prelims-relevant point. Footnotes are explanatory notes at the bottom of a table that clarify a specific point or entry in it.

stem: A diagram/graph that uses rectangular bars (of equal width, with heights/lengths proportional to the values) to represent and compare data is a:
solution: A bar diagram (bar graph) is a diagram that uses rectangular bars — of equal width, with equal spacing between them, and with the heights (or lengths) of the bars proportional to the values they represent — to represent and compare data. The bars can be vertical or horizontal. Bar diagrams are used to compare the values of different categories/items (e.g., the population of different states, or the sales in different years) — the taller/longer the bar, the greater the value, so comparisons are seen at a glance. (In a bar diagram, only the length/height matters, and the bars are usually separated by gaps.) Understanding the bar diagram is a prelims-relevant point. A bar diagram (bar graph) uses rectangular bars of equal width, with heights proportional to the values, to represent and compare data.

stem: A circular diagram divided into sectors ('slices'), where each sector's size represents the proportion/share of a category in the whole, is called a:
solution: A pie diagram (pie chart) is a circular diagram divided into sectors or 'slices', in which each sector represents a category/component, and the size of each sector (its angle/area) is proportional to the share/proportion of that category in the whole (the total, represented by the full circle of 360°). Pie charts are used to show how a total is divided into its component parts — i.e., the relative proportions/percentages of the different parts of a whole (for example, the breakdown of a budget, or the shares of different sources in total revenue). The whole circle = 100% (or 360°), and each slice = that category's share. Understanding the pie diagram is a prelims-relevant point. A pie diagram (pie chart) is a circle divided into sectors, each representing a category's proportion/share of the whole.

stem: In a pie chart, the whole circle represents the total (100%), which corresponds to __________ degrees.
solution: In a pie chart, the whole circle represents the total (100% of the data), and a full circle corresponds to 360 degrees. So, to draw a pie chart, the total (100%) is equated to 360°, and each category's share is converted into a proportionate angle at the centre: the angle for a category = (that category's value ÷ total) × 360°. For example, a category that is 25% of the total would get 25% of 360° = 90° (a quarter of the circle). This is how the circle is divided into proportionate sectors. Understanding that the full circle = 360° (= 100%) in a pie chart is a prelims-relevant point. In a pie chart, the whole circle (the total/100%) corresponds to 360 degrees.

stem: A graph that shows how a variable changes over time (with time on the horizontal axis), useful for showing trends, is a:
solution: A line graph (time series graph) is a graph that shows how a variable changes over time — with time (years, months, etc.) plotted on the horizontal (x) axis and the values of the variable on the vertical (y) axis, and the plotted points joined by a line. Line graphs are especially useful for showing trends — the rise and fall of a variable over a period (for example, how population, prices, or production have changed over the years) — and for spotting patterns and making comparisons over time. The slope/direction of the line shows whether the variable is increasing, decreasing, or fluctuating. Understanding the line graph (for time trends) is a prelims-relevant point. A line graph (time series graph) shows how a variable changes over time (time on the x-axis), useful for showing trends.

stem: A graph used to represent a CONTINUOUS grouped frequency distribution, using adjacent rectangles (with no gaps between them) whose areas represent the class frequencies, is a:
solution: A histogram is a graph used to represent a continuous grouped frequency distribution. It uses adjacent rectangles — one for each class interval — placed side by side with NO gaps between them (because the classes are continuous), where the width of each rectangle represents the class interval and the height represents the frequency (so that the area of each rectangle is proportional to the class frequency). The histogram thus shows the shape of the frequency distribution (where the data cluster and how they are spread) visually. (It differs from a bar diagram in that its bars are adjacent — no gaps — and it represents continuous class-interval data, with area representing frequency.) Understanding the histogram is a prelims-relevant point. A histogram represents a continuous grouped frequency distribution using adjacent rectangles (no gaps), whose areas represent the class frequencies.

stem: A key difference between a HISTOGRAM and a BAR diagram is that in a histogram the bars are __________ (touching, with no gaps), whereas in a bar diagram they usually have gaps between them.
solution: A key difference between a histogram and a bar diagram is the spacing of the bars: in a histogram, the bars (rectangles) are adjacent — they touch each other, with NO gaps between them — because the histogram represents continuous class-interval data (the classes are continuous, so the rectangles must be continuous too); whereas in a bar diagram, the bars usually have gaps/spaces between them, because a bar diagram represents distinct, separate categories (which are not continuous). (Another difference: in a histogram the area of each bar represents the frequency, and the width matters; in a bar diagram only the height/length represents the value, and the width is uniform and immaterial.) Understanding this histogram-vs-bar-diagram difference (adjacent vs gapped bars) is a prelims-relevant point. In a histogram the bars are adjacent (touching, no gaps), whereas in a bar diagram they usually have gaps between them.

stem: A graph obtained by joining the MIDPOINTS of the tops of the rectangles of a histogram (by straight lines) is called a frequency:
solution: A frequency polygon is a graph obtained by joining, with straight lines, the midpoints of the tops of the rectangles of a histogram (i.e., plotting a point at the top-middle of each histogram bar — at the class midpoint and the class frequency — and joining these points by straight lines). It is usually closed at both ends by extending the line to the midpoints of the (imaginary) classes just before the first and just after the last class (on the x-axis). A frequency polygon is another way (besides the histogram) of showing the shape of a frequency distribution, and it is useful for comparing two or more distributions on the same graph. Understanding the frequency polygon is a prelims-relevant point. A frequency polygon is obtained by joining the midpoints of the tops of the histogram rectangles with straight lines.

stem: The graph of a cumulative frequency distribution (a curve showing 'less than' or 'more than' cumulative frequencies) is called an:
solution: An ogive (also called a cumulative frequency curve) is the graph of a cumulative frequency distribution. It is drawn by plotting the cumulative frequencies (either 'less than' or 'more than') against the class limits and joining the points by a smooth curve. There are two types: the 'less than' ogive (rising curve, plotting 'less than' cumulative frequencies against upper class limits) and the 'more than' ogive (falling curve, plotting 'more than' cumulative frequencies against lower class limits). Ogives are useful for finding positional values like the median and quartiles graphically, and for finding how many observations lie below/above a given value. Understanding the ogive (cumulative frequency curve) is a prelims-relevant point. An ogive (cumulative frequency curve) is the graph of a cumulative frequency distribution ('less than' or 'more than').

stem: Diagrammatic/graphical presentation of data is advantageous because it:
options: is attractive and makes the data quickly and easily understandable at a glance (revealing patterns, trends, and comparisons visually)
solution: Diagrammatic/graphical presentation of data (using bar diagrams, pie charts, line graphs, histograms, etc.) is advantageous because it: is visually attractive and appealing (drawing attention and interest); makes the data quickly and easily understandable at a glance (a picture conveys the message faster and more clearly than a table of figures); reveals patterns, trends, comparisons, and relationships visually (which may be hard to see in raw figures); simplifies complex data; is easy to remember (a visual impression lasts); and can be understood even by those who are not experts with numbers. So diagrams/graphs make data communication effective and easy. (Their limitation is that they show only a general/approximate picture, not exact figures.) Understanding the advantages of graphical presentation is a prelims-relevant point. Graphical presentation is attractive and makes data quickly and easily understandable at a glance, revealing patterns, trends, and comparisons.

stem: A LIMITATION of diagrammatic/graphical presentation (compared to a table) is that:
options: it gives only a general/approximate picture, not the exact figures (and can even mislead if drawn improperly)
it is always better in every way
solution: A limitation of diagrammatic/graphical presentation (compared to tabular presentation) is that it gives only a general, approximate picture/impression of the data — not the exact, precise figures. From a graph or diagram, you can see the overall pattern, trend, or comparison, but you usually cannot read off the exact numerical values accurately (whereas a table gives the precise figures). Moreover, diagrams can even be misleading if they are drawn improperly or deliberately distorted (e.g., misusing the scale) — creating a false impression. So diagrams are good for a quick, visual overview but not for exact detail (for which tables are better). Understanding this limitation of graphs is a prelims-relevant point. A limitation of graphical presentation is that it gives only a general/approximate picture, not exact figures, and can mislead if drawn improperly.

stem: To compare the components/parts of two or more totals (e.g., the make-up of a budget in two years), a suitable diagram is a __________ bar diagram.
solution: A sub-divided (or component) bar diagram is a suitable diagram for comparing the components/parts of a total — and for comparing such component make-ups across two or more totals. In a sub-divided bar diagram, each bar (representing a total) is divided into segments/parts, with the length of each segment proportional to the value of that component, so that you can see both the total (the whole bar) and its components (the segments), and compare the composition of different totals (different bars). For example, the components of a family's expenditure (food, rent, etc.) in two different years can be shown as two sub-divided bars, one per year. Understanding the sub-divided/component bar diagram is a prelims-relevant point. A sub-divided (component) bar diagram compares the components/parts of two or more totals (each bar divided into proportional segments).

stem: A bar diagram in which several bars are grouped together side by side (to compare several related items across categories) is called a __________ bar diagram.
solution: A multiple (grouped/compound) bar diagram is a bar diagram in which two or more bars are grouped together side by side within each category (with different bars, usually in different colours/shades, representing different items/variables), so that several related items can be compared across the categories. For example, to compare the imports AND exports of a country over several years, each year would have two bars side by side (one for imports, one for exports). Multiple bar diagrams are used to compare more than one set of related data across categories. (This differs from the sub-divided bar diagram, where the components are stacked within a single bar.) Understanding the multiple/grouped bar diagram is a prelims-relevant point. A multiple (grouped) bar diagram groups several bars side by side to compare several related items across categories.

stem: Assertion (A): Data are often presented in tables and diagrams rather than left as raw figures. Reason (R): Tables and diagrams make the data more organised, clear, attractive, and easier to understand, compare, and interpret. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that data are usually presented in tables and diagrams/graphs, rather than being left as raw figures. And the reason is (R) that tables and diagrams make the data more organised, clear, attractive, and much easier to understand, compare, and interpret than a confusing mass of raw figures — a table arranges the figures systematically for easy reading and comparison, and a diagram/graph shows the patterns and trends visually at a glance. Because presentation in tables and diagrams is exactly what makes the data comprehensible and effective to communicate, this is why data are so presented — R correctly explains A. Understanding why data are presented in tables/diagrams is a prelims-relevant point. Data are presented in tables and diagrams because these make the data more organised, clear, attractive, and easier to understand, compare, and interpret.

stem: In a statistical table, the headings/titles of the ROWS (describing what each row contains) are called the:
solution: In a statistical table, the headings/titles given to the rows (the descriptions of what each row contains, usually written down the left-hand side) are called the 'stubs' (row headings). The headings of the columns (the descriptions of what each column contains, written across the top) are called the 'captions' (column headings). And the main part of the table, containing the actual data/figures (in the cells formed by the rows and columns), is called the 'body' of the table. So the stub = row headings, and the caption = column headings. Understanding the parts of a table (stub, caption, body) is a prelims-relevant point. In a table, the headings of the rows are called the stubs (and the headings of the columns are called captions).

stem: In a statistical table, the headings/titles of the COLUMNS are called the:
solution: In a statistical table, the headings/titles given to the columns (describing what each column contains, written across the top of the columns) are called the 'captions' (or column headings). (The headings of the rows — down the left side — are called the 'stubs'.) The captions and stubs together label the data so that the reader knows what each figure in the body of the table represents. So the caption = column heading. Understanding the caption (column heading) is a prelims-relevant point. In a table, the headings of the columns are called the captions (column headings).

stem: The main part of a table that contains the actual numerical data (in the cells) is called the __________ of the table.
solution: The 'body' of a table is the main part that contains the actual numerical data/figures — arranged in the cells formed by the intersection of the rows and the columns. It is the most important part of the table (the reason the table exists — to present these figures), organised according to the row headings (stubs) and column headings (captions). So the body = the data-filled main part of the table. (Other parts include the title, table number, head-note, stubs, captions, footnotes, and source.) Understanding the body of a table is a prelims-relevant point. The body of a table is the main part containing the actual numerical data (in the cells).

stem: A table constructed to present GENERAL information (a wide range of data, for reference), often large, is called a __________ table.
solution: A general-purpose table (also called a reference table) is a table constructed to present a wide range of general information/data for reference — it stores a large amount of data (often in big, detailed tables, like those in census reports or statistical abstracts), from which readers can look up whatever figures they need. It is not meant to make any particular point, but to serve as a source of data. (This contrasts with a 'special-purpose table' — also called a summary or text table — which is a smaller table designed to bring out and emphasise a specific point/comparison for a particular analysis or discussion.) Understanding general-purpose vs special-purpose tables is a prelims-relevant point. A general-purpose (reference) table presents a wide range of general data for reference, often in large tables.

stem: A tabulation in which the data are classified according to only ONE characteristic is called __________ tabulation.
solution: One-way tabulation (simple tabulation) is a tabulation in which the data are classified according to only one characteristic/variable. For example, a table showing just the number of students in each mark-range (classifying only by marks) is a one-way table. (If the data are classified by two characteristics together — e.g., by marks AND by gender — it is a 'two-way' table; and by more than two, a 'manifold'/complex table.) So one-way tabulation involves a single basis of classification. Understanding one-way (simple) tabulation is a prelims-relevant point. One-way (simple) tabulation classifies the data according to only one characteristic.

stem: A tabulation in which the data are classified according to TWO characteristics simultaneously (like students by both gender and marks) is called __________ tabulation.
solution: Two-way tabulation is a tabulation in which the data are classified according to two characteristics/variables at the same time (simultaneously) — shown in a two-way table (with one classification along the rows and the other along the columns). For example, a table showing the number of students classified by both their gender (rows) and their marks-range (columns) is a two-way table. Two-way tabulation lets us study two variables together (and any relationship between them). (Classifying by more than two characteristics gives 'manifold'/complex tables.) Understanding two-way tabulation is a prelims-relevant point. Two-way tabulation classifies the data according to two characteristics simultaneously (e.g., students by both gender and marks).

stem: A method of presenting data using PICTURES/symbols (where each picture represents a certain quantity) is called a:
solution: A pictogram (or pictograph) is a method of presenting data using pictures/symbols (small figures/icons representing the thing being measured), where each picture stands for a certain fixed quantity, and the number (or size) of the pictures represents the value. For example, to show the population of different countries, one might use a symbol of a person to represent, say, 1 crore people, and draw as many such symbols as needed for each country. Pictograms are visually appealing, simple, and easily understood (even by non-experts/the general public), which makes them popular for presenting data to a wide audience. (Their limitation: they show only approximate values, and part-symbols are hard to draw/read exactly.) Understanding pictograms is a prelims-relevant point. A pictogram (pictograph) presents data using pictures/symbols, each representing a certain quantity.

stem: A method of presenting data on a MAP (showing how a value varies over different geographical areas, e.g., by shading) is called a __________ (or choropleth map).
solution: A cartogram (or statistical map / choropleth map) is a method of presenting data on a map — showing how a value/quantity varies over different geographical areas (regions, states, countries). This is done by devices such as shading/colouring the areas (with darker shades for higher values — a 'choropleth' map), or by placing dots, figures, or symbols on the areas in proportion to their values. For example, a map of India shaded to show the population density (or literacy rate) of each state is a cartogram. Cartograms are useful for showing the geographical/spatial distribution of a variable at a glance. Understanding cartograms/statistical maps is a prelims-relevant point. A cartogram (statistical map / choropleth map) presents data on a map, showing how a value varies over different geographical areas.

stem: On a graph, the horizontal axis (the x-axis) is called the __________ and the vertical axis (the y-axis) is called the ordinate.
solution: On a graph (a two-dimensional coordinate graph), the horizontal axis (the x-axis) is called the 'abscissa', and the vertical axis (the y-axis) is called the 'ordinate'. (The point where the two axes meet/cross is the 'origin'.) The value of the independent variable (like time) is usually measured along the x-axis (abscissa), and the value of the dependent variable along the y-axis (ordinate). So: abscissa = x-axis (horizontal); ordinate = y-axis (vertical). Understanding these terms (abscissa and ordinate) is a prelims-relevant point. On a graph, the horizontal (x) axis is the abscissa and the vertical (y) axis is the ordinate.

stem: The point where the two axes of a graph meet (the zero point, coordinates 0,0) is called the:
solution: The origin is the point where the two axes of a graph (the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis) meet/intersect — the zero point, with coordinates (0, 0). From the origin, values are measured to the right (positive x) and upward (positive y) — and, in a full coordinate plane, also to the left (negative x) and downward (negative y). The origin is the reference/starting point for plotting points on the graph. Understanding the origin (the (0,0) point where the axes meet) is a prelims-relevant point. The origin is the point where the two axes of a graph meet (the zero point, coordinates 0,0).

stem: In drawing a pie chart, a category that forms 25% of the total is shown by a sector with a central angle of:
solution: In a pie chart, the whole circle (the total, 100%) equals 360°, so each category's share is converted into a proportionate central angle: angle = (category's percentage ÷ 100) × 360°. For a category forming 25% of the total: angle = (25 ÷ 100) × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°. So a 25% category is shown by a sector with a central angle of 90° (a quarter of the circle) — which makes sense, since 25% is one-quarter of the whole. (A useful shortcut: each 1% corresponds to 3.6°, so 25% × 3.6° = 90°.) Understanding how to convert a percentage into a pie-chart angle (with this example) is a prelims-relevant point. In a pie chart, a category that is 25% of the total is shown by a sector of central angle 25% × 360° = 90°.

stem: In converting percentages to pie-chart angles, each 1% of the total corresponds to __________ degrees.
solution: In converting percentages into pie-chart angles, each 1% of the total corresponds to 3.6 degrees. This is because the whole (100%) equals 360°, so 1% = 360° ÷ 100 = 3.6°. Therefore, to find the angle for any category, you can multiply its percentage by 3.6° (e.g., 20% → 20 × 3.6° = 72°; 50% → 50 × 3.6° = 180°). This '3.6° per 1%' rule is a handy shortcut for drawing pie charts. Understanding this conversion factor (1% = 3.6°) is a prelims-relevant point. In a pie chart, each 1% of the total corresponds to 3.6 degrees (since 100% = 360°).

stem: A bar diagram (with only length representing the value) is an example of a __________ diagram.
solution: A bar diagram is an example of a one-dimensional diagram — because only one dimension of the bar (its length/height) is used to represent the value/magnitude of the data (the width of the bars is kept uniform and is not meaningful). So the value is shown by length alone (one dimension). (In contrast: 'two-dimensional' diagrams — like rectangles, squares, circles/pie charts — use area, i.e., two dimensions, to represent values; and 'three-dimensional' diagrams — like cubes, cylinders, spheres — use volume.) So bar diagrams and line diagrams are one-dimensional. Understanding that a bar diagram is one-dimensional (length represents value) is a prelims-relevant point. A bar diagram is a one-dimensional diagram, because only the length/height of the bar represents the value.

stem: Diagrams like circles/pie charts and rectangles, in which the AREA represents the value, are called __________ diagrams.
solution: Diagrams like circles (pie charts), squares, and rectangles — in which the area (two dimensions) is used to represent the value/magnitude of the data — are called two-dimensional diagrams (also called 'area diagrams'). Here it is the area of the figure (not just a length) that is made proportional to the value. (This contrasts with 'one-dimensional' diagrams — like bars/lines, where only length represents the value — and 'three-dimensional' diagrams — like cubes and cylinders, where volume represents the value.) So pie charts and rectangles are two-dimensional (area) diagrams. Understanding two-dimensional (area) diagrams is a prelims-relevant point. Diagrams like circles/pie charts and rectangles, where the area represents the value, are two-dimensional (area) diagrams.

stem: The textual (descriptive) method of presenting data is most suitable when:
options: there is a huge amount of numerical data
the amount of data is small (a few figures), or the data are to be emphasised/highlighted in the discussion
the data must be shown visually
solution: The textual (descriptive) method of presenting data — presenting the figures within the running text/paragraphs (describing them in words) — is most suitable when: the amount of data is small (only a few figures, which can be conveniently woven into the text); or when particular figures are to be emphasised/highlighted and discussed in the accompanying narrative. Its advantage is that it can add emphasis and explanation. Its disadvantage: it is unsuitable for large amounts of data (a lot of figures buried in the text become confusing and hard to compare — a table or diagram would be far better). So text is best for small data or emphasis, not for large data sets. Understanding when textual presentation is suitable is a prelims-relevant point. Textual presentation is most suitable when the amount of data is small, or when data are to be emphasised in the discussion.

stem: A good diagram/graph should have a clear __________, an appropriate scale, correct proportions, and be neat and simple.
solution: A good diagram/graph should have certain requisites/features to be effective, including: a clear, brief, self-explanatory title (telling what the diagram is about); an appropriate scale (chosen so the diagram fits the space and shows the data proportionately, with the scale clearly stated); correct proportions (the sizes/lengths accurately proportional to the values, so as not to mislead); an index/legend/key (where different shades or colours are used, to explain what they mean); proper labelling of axes/parts; and being neat, simple, clean, and attractive (not cluttered or confusing). Following these ensures the diagram conveys the data accurately and clearly. Understanding the requisites of a good diagram is a prelims-relevant point. A good diagram should have a clear title, an appropriate scale, correct proportions, a legend where needed, and be neat and simple.

stem: The 'less than' ogive and the 'more than' ogive, when drawn together, intersect at a point whose x-value gives the __________ of the distribution.
solution: When both the 'less than' ogive (rising curve) and the 'more than' ogive (falling curve) are drawn on the same graph, they intersect (cross) at a point; the x-coordinate (the value on the horizontal axis) of this point of intersection gives the median of the distribution. This is a graphical method of finding the median from a cumulative frequency distribution. (The median is the middle value, and it makes sense that the point where the 'number of values below' equals the 'number of values above' — i.e., where the two ogives cross — corresponds to the median.) Understanding that the ogives intersect at the median is a prelims-relevant point. The 'less than' and 'more than' ogives intersect at a point whose x-value gives the median of the distribution.

stem: When a graph's vertical scale does not start at zero, a __________ (a break/zigzag near the origin) is used to show that the scale has been broken (to avoid misleading the reader).
solution: When the values to be plotted on a graph are all large and close together (far from zero), the vertical scale may be made to start not from zero but from a higher value (to show the variation clearly without a huge empty space) — but this can mislead the reader (exaggerating the differences). To indicate honestly that the scale does NOT start at zero (that a part of the scale has been omitted/broken), a 'false base line' is used — shown by a break or zigzag/kink mark near the origin (at the bottom of the vertical axis). This alerts the reader that the scale is broken, preventing a misleading impression. Understanding the false base line (scale-break) is a prelims-relevant point. A false base line (a break/zigzag near the origin) is used when the vertical scale does not start at zero, to show honestly that the scale has been broken.

stem: When drawing a histogram for a frequency distribution with UNEQUAL class intervals, the heights of the rectangles must be adjusted so that the __________ (not the height) is proportional to the frequency.
solution: When drawing a histogram for a frequency distribution with unequal (varying) class intervals, the heights of the rectangles must be adjusted so that the AREA of each rectangle (not just its height) is proportional to the class frequency. This is because, in a histogram, it is the area (width × height) that represents the frequency. If the class widths are equal, then the heights can simply equal the frequencies (since the widths are the same); but if the widths are unequal, using the raw frequencies as heights would distort the picture (a wider class would look bigger than it should). So the heights are adjusted (dividing the frequency by the class width to get the 'frequency density') so that area = frequency. Understanding this adjustment (area ∝ frequency for unequal classes) is a prelims-relevant point. For unequal class intervals in a histogram, the heights are adjusted so that the area (not the height) of each rectangle is proportional to the frequency.

stem: A tabular presentation is generally preferred over a diagram when the reader needs to know the __________.
solution: Tabular presentation (a table) is generally preferred over a diagram/graph when the reader needs to know the exact numerical figures/values — because a table gives the precise, exact figures (which can be read off directly and used for further calculation), whereas a diagram/graph gives only a general, approximate visual impression (from which exact values usually cannot be read accurately). So, for detail and precision, tables are better; for a quick visual overview of patterns/trends, diagrams are better. They complement each other (a table can be presented alongside a diagram). Understanding when a table is preferred (for exact figures) is a prelims-relevant point. A table is preferred over a diagram when the reader needs the exact numerical figures/values.

stem: A frequency distribution can be graphically represented, and the histogram can also be used to locate the __________ of the distribution graphically.
solution: The histogram of a frequency distribution can be used to locate the mode of the distribution graphically. The mode is the value that occurs most frequently — corresponding to the tallest rectangle (the class with the highest frequency, the 'modal class') in the histogram. To find the mode graphically: in the histogram, draw lines from the top corners of the tallest (modal) rectangle to the corresponding top corners of the two adjacent rectangles (crossing diagonally); the point where these two lines intersect, dropped down to the x-axis, gives the value of the mode. So the histogram is a graphical tool for locating the mode. Understanding that the histogram gives the mode graphically is a prelims-relevant point. The histogram can be used to locate the mode of the distribution graphically (from the tallest/modal rectangle).

stem: A 'percentage bar diagram' (each bar totalling 100%, divided into components) is useful for comparing the __________ composition of different totals.
solution: A percentage bar diagram (a special kind of sub-divided/component bar diagram) is one in which each bar is drawn to the same total height, representing 100%, and is divided into segments showing the PERCENTAGE share of each component. It is useful for comparing the percentage/relative composition (the proportional make-up) of different totals — because, by making every bar equal to 100%, it lets you compare the shares of the components across the different bars directly (regardless of the different absolute sizes of the totals). For example, to compare how the percentage breakdown of expenditure (food, rent, etc.) differs between two families of different total incomes, a percentage bar diagram is ideal. Understanding the percentage bar diagram (for comparing relative composition) is a prelims-relevant point. A percentage bar diagram (each bar = 100%, divided into components) compares the percentage/relative composition of different totals.

stem: The 'head-note' of a table (given below the title) is used to:
options: give additional explanation about the table's contents (like the units of measurement) that could not fit in the title
solution: The 'head-note' of a table — a note given just below the title (usually in brackets) — is used to provide additional explanatory information about the table's contents that could not be conveniently included in the title, most commonly the units of measurement of the data (for example, '(in ₹ crore)', '(in thousands)', or '(figures in percentages)'). The head-note thus tells the reader important information (like the units) needed to correctly read and interpret the figures in the table. So the head-note supplements the title with such details. Understanding the head-note of a table is a prelims-relevant point. The head-note (below the title) gives additional explanation about the table's contents, such as the units of measurement.

stem: Which diagram is MOST suitable for showing the percentage break-up of a single total into its parts (like how a rupee of the government's income is spent)?
solution: The pie diagram (pie chart) is the most suitable diagram for showing the percentage break-up/composition of a single total into its component parts — such as how each rupee of the government's income is spent among the different heads, or the breakdown of a budget or expenditure. The pie chart's circle represents the whole (the total, 100%), and each slice/sector shows the proportion/share of one component — so the relative sizes of the parts (and their shares of the whole) are seen clearly at a glance. So, for showing the components/proportions of a single whole, the pie chart is ideal. (Bar diagrams are better for comparing values across categories; line graphs for trends over time.) Understanding when to use a pie chart is a prelims-relevant point. A pie diagram (pie chart) is most suitable for showing the percentage break-up of a single total into its component parts.

stem: When comparing data for many years to show a TREND over time, the most suitable graph is a:
solution: When comparing data over many years (or other time periods) to show a trend over time — the way a variable rises, falls, or fluctuates through time — the most suitable graph is a line graph (time series graph). By plotting the values against time and joining them with a line, the line graph clearly shows the overall trend and pattern over the period (and can compare several trends on one graph). It is far better for showing time trends than, say, a pie chart (which shows composition, not trends over time) or many separate bars. So, for trends over time, use a line graph. Understanding when to use a line graph (for time trends) is a prelims-relevant point. To show a trend over many years/time periods, the most suitable graph is a line graph (time series graph).

stem: The proper choice of __________ (the ratio between the units on the graph and the actual values) is important when drawing a graph, so that the data are shown clearly and without distortion.
solution: The proper choice of scale — the ratio between the units marked on the graph's axes and the actual values they represent (e.g., '1 cm = 10 units') — is important when drawing a graph. A suitable scale ensures that the data fit neatly in the available space and are shown clearly and proportionately (accurately), without distortion. A badly chosen scale can either cram the data (making differences hard to see) or exaggerate/misrepresent them (misleading the reader — a common way graphs are misused). The scale should be chosen appropriately and clearly indicated on the graph. Understanding the importance of the scale is a prelims-relevant point. The proper choice of scale (the ratio between graph units and actual values) is important so that the data are shown clearly and without distortion.

stem: The advantages of tabular presentation include that it condenses the data, facilitates comparison, saves space, and:
options: makes the exact figures easy to locate, read, and use for further analysis
solution: The advantages of tabular presentation (presenting data in tables) include: it condenses a large mass of data into a compact, organised form; it facilitates comparison (data arranged in rows and columns can be readily compared across categories, groups, or periods); it saves space (a table holds a lot of data compactly, more than the same data described in text would); and it makes the exact figures easy to locate, read, and use — one can quickly find any specific value, and the precise figures are available for further statistical analysis and calculation. Tables also present the data neatly and systematically. So tabulation makes data organised, comparable, compact, and readily usable. Understanding the advantages of tabulation is a prelims-relevant point. Tabular presentation condenses the data, facilitates comparison, saves space, and makes the exact figures easy to locate, read, and use.

stem: Assertion (A): A diagram/graph should be drawn with correct proportions and an honest scale. Reason (R): An improperly drawn or distorted diagram (e.g., with a misleading scale) can create a false impression and mislead the reader. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that a diagram/graph should be drawn with correct proportions and an honest (appropriate, undistorted) scale. And the reason is (R) that an improperly drawn or deliberately distorted diagram — for example, one using a misleading scale (like a broken or exaggerated scale without indicating it), or with parts not drawn in true proportion — can create a false impression and mislead the reader (making differences look bigger or smaller than they really are, or suggesting a wrong pattern). Because a distorted diagram misleads, it follows that diagrams must be drawn honestly and proportionately to convey the true picture — so R correctly explains why correct proportions and an honest scale are needed (A). (This is one of the ways statistics/graphs can be misused.) Understanding this is a prelims-relevant point. Diagrams must be drawn with correct proportions and an honest scale because a distorted diagram can create a false impression and mislead the reader.

stem: A 'simple bar diagram' is used to present and compare data classified according to:
options: two or more characteristics at once
a single characteristic (one set of values across categories)
solution: A simple bar diagram is used to present and compare data classified according to a single characteristic — i.e., one set of values across a number of categories (each category shown by one bar). For example, to compare the total population of different states (one value — population — for each state/category), a simple bar diagram (one bar per state) is used. (When there are two or more sets of related values to compare across categories, a multiple/grouped bar diagram is used; and when a total is to be broken into components, a sub-divided bar diagram is used.) So the simple bar diagram handles one variable across categories. Understanding the simple bar diagram is a prelims-relevant point. A simple bar diagram presents and compares data classified according to a single characteristic (one value across categories).

stem: Presentation of data means arranging the organised data in a form (tables, diagrams, graphs) that makes it:
options: clear, attractive and easy to understand, compare and interpret
solution: Presentation displays the organised data in tables, diagrams or graphs so that it becomes clear, attractive and easy to understand, compare and interpret.

stem: The three main forms of presenting data are textual (descriptive), tabular, and __________ presentation.
solution: Data can be presented textually (in paragraphs), in tables, or through diagrams and graphs.

stem: In a statistical table, the vertical arrangements of data are called:
solution: In a table, the horizontal arrangements are rows and the vertical arrangements are columns.

stem: The headings/titles of the ROWS in a table (describing what each row contains) are called the:
solution: The row headings of a table are called stubs; the column headings are called captions.

stem: The headings/titles of the COLUMNS in a table are called the:
solution: The column headings of a table are called captions (and the row headings are stubs).

stem: Every statistical table must have a __________ that clearly states what the table is about.
solution: A table must have a clear, concise title stating what it presents.

stem: The __________ of a table (given at the bottom) states where the data came from.
solution: The source note at the foot of a table indicates the origin of the data, allowing verification.

stem: Explanatory notes at the bottom of a table that clarify a specific entry or point are called:
solution: Footnotes explain or qualify particular items/entries in the table that need clarification.

stem: A tabulation classifying data according to TWO characteristics simultaneously (like students by gender AND marks) is called __________ tabulation.
solution: Double (two-way) tabulation classifies data by two characteristics at the same time.

stem: A large table constructed to present GENERAL information (a wide range of data, for reference) is called a __________ table.
solution: A general-purpose (reference) table presents a wide range of data for general reference, whereas a special-purpose (summary/text) table highlights a particular relationship.

stem: A diagram using rectangular bars of equal width, with heights proportional to the values, to compare data is a:
solution: A bar diagram uses equal-width rectangular bars whose heights (lengths) are proportional to the values, for comparison.

stem: A 'simple bar diagram' is used to present data classified according to:
solution: A simple bar diagram represents data classified by a single characteristic (one variable), e.g., the population of different states.

stem: A bar diagram in which several bars are grouped side by side to compare related items across categories is a __________ bar diagram.
solution: A multiple (grouped) bar diagram places several bars side by side within each category to compare related items (e.g., exports and imports over years).

stem: A bar in which the total is subdivided into its component parts (each part shown as a segment of the bar) is a __________ bar diagram.
solution: A component (sub-divided) bar diagram divides each bar into segments representing the components of the total.

stem: A circular diagram divided into sectors, where each sector's size represents a category's share of the whole, is called a:
solution: A pie chart (pie diagram) is a circle divided into sectors whose angles/areas represent the proportions of the categories in the total.

stem: In a pie chart, the whole circle (representing the total, or 100%) corresponds to __________ degrees.
solution: The full circle of a pie chart represents the total (100%) and corresponds to 360 degrees.

stem: In a pie chart, a category forming 25% of the total is shown by a sector with a central angle of:
A graph showing how a variable changes over time (time on the horizontal axis), useful for trends, is a:
solution: A line graph (time-series graph) plots a variable against time and is ideal for showing trends over time.

stem: A graph representing a CONTINUOUS grouped frequency distribution using adjacent rectangles (no gaps) whose areas represent the frequencies is a:
solution: A histogram represents a continuous grouped frequency distribution with adjacent rectangles (no gaps) whose areas are proportional to the class frequencies.

stem: A key difference between a histogram and a bar diagram is that in a histogram the bars are __________.
solution: In a histogram the rectangles touch (no gaps, because the classes are continuous), whereas bar-diagram bars usually have gaps between them.

stem: The graph obtained by joining the MIDPOINTS of the tops of the histogram rectangles by straight lines is called a frequency:
solution: A frequency polygon is formed by joining the midpoints of the tops of the histogram's rectangles with straight lines.

stem: The graph of a cumulative frequency distribution ('less than' or 'more than') is called an:
solution: An ogive is the cumulative frequency curve, drawn by plotting cumulative frequencies against class boundaries.

stem: The 'less than' ogive and the 'more than' ogive, drawn together, intersect at a point whose x-value gives the __________ of the distribution.
solution: The x-coordinate of the point where the two ogives intersect gives the median of the distribution.

stem: A method of presenting data using PICTURES/symbols, where each picture represents a certain quantity, is called a:
solution: A pictogram (pictograph) presents data using pictures or symbols, each representing a fixed quantity.

stem: A method of presenting data on a MAP (showing how a value varies over geographical areas, e.g., by shading) is called a:
solution: A cartogram (choropleth map) shows how a value varies across geographical areas, typically using shading or symbols on a map.

stem: On a graph, the horizontal axis (x-axis) is called the __________.
solution: The horizontal axis (x-axis) is the abscissa; the vertical axis (y-axis) is the ordinate.

stem: The point where the two axes of a graph meet (coordinates 0,0) is called the:
solution: The origin is the point (0,0) where the x-axis and y-axis intersect.

stem: A bar diagram, in which only the LENGTH (one dimension) represents the value, is an example of a __________ diagram.
solution: A bar diagram is a one-dimensional diagram, since only the length of the bar represents the value (the width is uniform and immaterial).

stem: Diagrams like pie charts and rectangles, in which the AREA represents the value, are called __________ diagrams.
solution: Two-dimensional diagrams (rectangles, squares, circles/pie charts) represent values by area.

stem: When drawing a histogram for a frequency distribution with UNEQUAL class intervals, the heights must be adjusted so that the __________ is proportional to the frequency.
solution: For unequal class intervals, the rectangle heights are adjusted (using frequency density) so that the AREA (not the height) is proportional to the class frequency.

stem: When a graph's vertical scale does not start at zero, a __________ is used near the origin to show the scale has been broken.
solution: A false base line (a break or zigzag near the origin) shows that the vertical scale has been broken (does not start at zero), to avoid misleading the reader.

stem: A LIMITATION of diagrammatic/graphical presentation (compared with a table) is that:
options: it gives only an approximate picture, not the exact figures
it takes more space than tables
solution: Diagrams show only an approximate, visual picture and cannot convey the exact figures that a table provides.

stem: Which diagram is MOST suitable for showing the percentage break-up of a single total into its parts (e.g., how a rupee of income is spent)?
solution: A pie chart is best for showing how a single total is divided into its component parts/percentages.

stem: The advantages of tabular presentation include that it condenses data, facilitates comparison, saves space, and:
options: makes the data ready for further statistical analysis and easy reference
solution: Tabulation condenses data, aids comparison, saves space and provides an organised basis for further analysis and easy reference.

stem: The proper choice of __________ (the ratio between graph units and actual values) is important so that data are shown clearly and without distortion.
solution: An appropriate scale (the ratio of graph units to actual values) is essential so that the graph represents the data clearly and honestly, without distortion.

stem: A good diagram/graph should have a clear title, an appropriate scale, correct proportions, and be:
solution: A good diagram must be neat, simple, clearly titled, correctly scaled and proportioned, with proper labels and an index/source.

stem: The head-note (given below the title of a table) is used to:
options: provide additional explanation about the table as a whole (like the unit of measurement)
solution: The head-note, placed below the title, gives supplementary information about the table as a whole, such as the unit of measurement (e.g., 'in thousands').

stem: A histogram can also be used to locate the __________ of a distribution graphically.
solution: The mode of a grouped frequency distribution can be located graphically from the histogram (by joining the corners of the tallest and adjacent rectangles).

stem: Diagrammatic presentation is advantageous because it:
options: gives a quick, attractive and easily grasped visual impression, aiding comparison
is always more precise than a table
solution: Diagrams give a quick, attractive and readily understood visual impression that makes comparison easy and leaves a lasting impact, though they are not exact.

stem: To compare the COMPONENTS of two or more totals (e.g., the make-up of budgets in two years), a suitable diagram is a __________ bar diagram.
solution: A component (sub-divided) bar diagram compares both the totals and their components across categories, ideal for comparing the make-up of two or more totals.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'Presentation of Data'?
options: Data should be left as raw figures
Well-designed tables, diagrams and graphs make data clear, comparable and easy to understand — but must be drawn honestly and appropriately
solution: The chapter concludes that appropriate and honestly-drawn tables, diagrams and graphs transform organised data into a clear, attractive and easily understood form, aiding comparison and interpretation.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Presentation of Data' is that:
options: Data should be left as raw figures

Organised data should be presented in a clear, attractive, and understandable form — through textual (descriptive), tabular (rows and columns, with title, headings, source, etc.), and diagrammatic/graphical (bar diagrams, pie charts, line graphs, histograms, frequency polygons, ogives) methods — so that the data's meaning, patterns, and comparisons can be readily grasped, with tables giving exact detail and diagrams giving a quick visual picture
solution: The chapter conveys that, once data have been collected and organised, they should be presented in a clear, attractive, and easily-understandable form, so that their meaning, patterns, and comparisons can be readily grasped by the reader. It explains the three main methods of presenting data: (1) textual (descriptive) presentation — presenting the data within the text/in words (suitable for small amounts of data or for emphasis); (2) tabular presentation — arranging the data systematically in tables (rows and columns), with the proper parts of a table (title, table number, head-note, column headings/captions, row headings/stubs, body, footnotes, and source) — which condenses the data into an orderly, detailed, and comparable form and gives the exact figures; and (3) diagrammatic/graphical presentation — showing the data through diagrams and graphs, such as bar diagrams (simple, multiple/grouped, and sub-divided/component), pie diagrams (pie charts, showing proportions of a whole, with the circle = 360° = 100%), line graphs (time-series graphs, showing trends over time), histograms (for continuous grouped frequency distributions, with adjacent rectangles whose areas show frequencies), frequency polygons (joining the midpoints of the histogram tops), and ogives (cumulative frequency curves) — which make the data visually attractive and quickly understandable, revealing patterns, trends, and comparisons at a glance. The chapter notes the advantages of graphical presentation (attractive, quick, and easy to understand, and good for revealing patterns/trends) and its limitation (it gives only a general/approximate picture, not exact figures, and can mislead if drawn improperly), so that tables (for exact detail) and diagrams (for a quick visual picture) complement each other. Understanding the methods of presenting data — textual, tabular, and diagrammatic/graphical — and when and how to use each is the central concern of this chapter. Organised data should be presented in clear, attractive form — through text, tables, and diagrams/graphs — so that its meaning, patterns, and comparisons are easily grasped, with tables giving exact detail and diagrams a quick visual picture.
